procedural_history.originating_court: First Special Tribunal Calcutta constituted under the Criminal Law Amendment Ordinance of 1943
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 5th June, 1953 of the High Court of Judicature for the State of West Bengal at Calcutta in Criminal Revisions Nos. 1205 and 1204 of 1952.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Appellants were convicted by the First Special Tribunal Calcutta. On appeal to the High Court of Calcutta, the High Court set aside the conviction on the ground that the Special Tribunal was not properly constituted. The High Court directed that the accused should be retried in accordance with law by a court of competent jurisdiction, leaving it to the State Government to decide whether the trial should proceed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeal by Special Leave granted by the Supreme Court by its Order dated the 14th September, 1953.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 12 of the West Bengal Act XII of 1952, which makes the Act inapplicable to cases pending before any other court on the date of its commencement, acts as a bar to the trial of the appellants by a Special Court under that Act, because their appeals were pending before the High Court on the said date.

facts: The appellants were convicted by a Special Tribunal constituted under a 1943 Central Ordinance.
They appealed this conviction to the High Court.
While their appeals were pending before the High Court, the West Bengal Act XII of 1952 came into force on April 9, 1952.
The High Court subsequently set aside the conviction, finding the original trial void, and ordered a retrial by a "court of competent jurisdiction".
The case was then allotted for retrial to a Special Court constituted under the new 1952 Act.
law: Section 12 of the West Bengal Act XII of 1952 states that the Act shall not apply to "any proceedings pending on the date of the commencement of the... Ordinance... in any court other than a Special Court".
The Supreme Court interpreted the phrase "proceedings in a court" in Section 12 to mean proceedings related to the trial of a case in an original court, not proceedings in an appeal.

The Court determined that the legislative object of Section 12 was to prevent ongoing trials in ordinary courts from being transferred to the new Special Courts, a reason that does not apply to appellate proceedings.
application: The Court first determined that what was pending before the High Court on the relevant date was an appeal, not an original trial.
Based on its interpretation of the law, the Court found that the pendency of an appeal did not trigger the bar created by Section 12, as that section was only concerned with pending trials.
The Court then examined the High Court's order for a retrial. The High Court had invalidated the original trial because the first tribunal was no longer a competent court.
Therefore, the High Court's direction for a retrial by a "competent court" could not mean a retrial by the original, now-invalid tribunal.

The only court competent to try the case was the new Special Court established under the 1952 Act. The High Court's order, by requiring a competent court, effectively directed the case to this new Special Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' contention, holding that Section 12 of the Act was not a bar to their trial. The Court reasoned that the "proceedings" mentioned in Section 12 refer to original trials, not appeals. Therefore, the fact that the appellants' appeals were pending when the Act commenced was irrelevant. The subsequent retrial in the Special Court was proper as it was the only competent court available to hear the case following the High Court's order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 12 of the West Bengal Act XII of 1952, which makes the Act inapplicable to cases pending before any other court on the date of its commencement, acts as a bar to the trial of the appellants by a Special Court under that Act, because their appeals were pending before the High Court on the said date.
appellant_arguments: Section 12 of the West Bengal Act XII of 1952 acts as a bar to their trial under the Act.
Their case was pending before the High Court in the form of an appeal on April 9, 1952, the date the preceding Ordinance commenced.
Because the case was pending, the provisions of the Act were made expressly inapplicable to it by Section 12.
The retrial ordered by the High Court is merely a continuation of the original case, which was initiated before the first Special Tribunal.
respondent_arguments: The pendency of an appeal before the High Court does not attract the operation of Section 12, which likely refers to cases pending for trial, not appeal.
The original trial court (Special Tribunal under the 1943 Ordinance) was declared to have lost its jurisdiction and become void after the Constitution came into force.
Since the original tribunal was no longer a valid court, the case could not be sent back to it for retrial.
The High Court directed a retrial by a 'competent court', and the only competent court to try the case was the new Special Court constituted under the 1952 Act.
The jurisdiction of the new Special Court cannot be ousted by Section 12 because the High Court's order itself was based on the fact that the original tribunal could no longer hold a trial.

statutes.act_name: West Bengal Criminal Law Amendment (Special Courts) Amending Ordinance 1952 (Ordinance VIII of 1952)

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The statutory phrase "proceedings pending... in any court other than a special court" refers to proceedings relating to the trial of a case in an original court and not to proceedings in an appellate court. Therefore, the pendency of an appeal does not, by itself, bar a special court from conducting a retrial ordered by the appellate court.
obiter: Ordinarily, an order of retrial means a further trial by the same tribunal which took cognizance of the case.
How a case is to proceed further if an appellate court directs a rehearing would depend entirely on the order which the appellate court passes and is competent in law to pass.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that Section 12 of the West Bengal Act XII of 1952, which makes the Act inapplicable to pending proceedings, refers exclusively to proceedings relating to the trial of a case in an original court, not to proceedings in appeal. Therefore, the pendency of the appellants' appeal before the High Court did not bar their retrial by a Special Court under the new Act. The jurisdiction of the new Special Court was affirmed because the High Court had ordered a retrial by a 'competent court', and the original tribunal had been rendered void and incompetent, leaving the new Special Court as the only legally competent forum for the trial.
legal_tests_applied: Purposive Interpretation of Statute: The court analyzed the legislative object of Section 12, concluding it was enacted to prevent the transfer of cases already being tried in ordinary courts to the new special courts, a purpose that has no application to cases pending on appeal.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's interpretation of Section 12, holding that the expression 'proceedings in a court other than a special court' refers to original trial proceedings, not appellate proceedings.

The argument that the retrial was a continuation of the original case failed because the High Court's own decision had rendered the original trial tribunal void and without jurisdiction as of January 26, 1950, making it impossible for the case to be sent back to it.

The pendency of the appeal itself did not attract the bar of Section 12, as the purpose of that section was to deal with ongoing trials at the original stage, not to dictate the forum for a retrial ordered by an appellate court.
why_respondent_won: The court determined that the nature and effect of the High Court's order for a retrial were paramount. The order directed a retrial by a 'competent court'.

The original Special Tribunal, from which the appeal was taken, was held to have lost its jurisdiction and become void after the Constitution came into force. Therefore, it was no longer a 'competent court' to which the case could be remanded.
As the original tribunal was legally defunct, the only court competent to try the case in accordance with the High Court's order was the new Special Court constituted under Act XII of 1952.
The jurisdiction of the new Special Court was not ousted by Section 12 because the High Court's order itself was premised on the fact that the original tribunal could no longer hold a valid trial.
policy_considerations: The court identified the legislative policy behind Section 12 as preventing the disruption of ongoing trials in ordinary courts by ensuring they would not be transferred to the new special courts, rather than creating a blanket bar on jurisdiction for any case that happened to be in the judicial system at any level.
